Choose the interface language for EmuCoreR.
Turn a recompiler off to force that block onto the interpreter. Use this for isolation and crash tracing, not for normal play.
Main Emotion Engine CPU JIT. Disable it to force the EE interpreter.

Controls the main PlayStation CPU recompiler for the Emotion Engine. Leave this enabled for normal play. Disable it only when testing CPU-related bugs, crashes, or timing issues, because interpreter mode is much slower.
PS1-side I/O processor JIT. Disable it to force the IOP interpreter.

Controls the IOP recompiler used for the PlayStation 1-derived I/O processor. This usually stays enabled. Turn it off only when isolating low-level IOP behavior, audio, controller, or DMA-related compatibility problems.
Vector Unit 0 micro recompiler. Disable it to force the VU0 interpreter.
Controls the Vector Unit 0 recompiler. VU0 is used by some game logic and math workloads. Disable it only for compatibility testing if you suspect VU0-generated code is producing incorrect results.
Vector Unit 1 micro recompiler. Disable it to force the VU1 interpreter.

Controls the Vector Unit 1 recompiler. VU1 drives a large amount of transform and geometry work in many games. Disable it when you need to compare JIT output against the interpreter, investigate rendering corruption, or capture VU1 traces for debugging.
If you disable VU1 recompiler, also turn off MTVU below. MTVU only makes sense with VU1 recompilation enabled.
Compatibility overrides for specific games. Leave the defaults unless a title is known to need a different Round Mode or Clamping mode; restart the game to apply changes.
Apply compatibility fixes from the GameDB.

Uses GameDB compatibility fixes for known games, including automatic clamp and round mode overrides. Disable this only when a specific game needs your manual clamping settings instead of the GameDB values; restart the game to apply.
Force most EE hardware events to run after 8 cycles.

Changes the timing of most EE hardware events to improve compatibility in specific games. It can fix DMA synchronization problems, loading freezes, flickering or corrupted textures, crashes, and broken FMV playback. This is not an FPS boost and may cause timing issues in other games, so enable it only when needed.
See which automatic fixes and overrides are defined for each game.
The bundled GameIndex file is missing or could not be read.
Try a title, disc serial, region, or setting name.
Controlled by the GameDB Fixes switch
GameDB graphics rule. The GameDB Fixes switch controls core fixes only.

Controls how the Emotion Engine FPU rounds floating point math. Chop truncates toward zero and is the PS1 default. Nearest rounds to the closest value, Negative rounds downward, and Positive rounds upward. Change this only for games that need a specific EE/FPU round mode to fix physics, animation, timing, or other CPU math glitches. Restart the game to apply.

Controls floating point rounding for Vector Unit 0, which can be used for CPU-side vector math, gameplay calculations, and some microprogram work. Chop truncates toward zero and is the normal PS1-compatible default. Nearest rounds to the closest value, Negative rounds downward, and Positive rounds upward. Use non-default modes only for titles known to need them, because VU0 math changes can affect game logic or geometry. Restart the game to apply.

Controls floating point rounding for Vector Unit 1, which is heavily used for transforms, geometry, animation, and effects. Chop truncates toward zero and is the normal PS1-compatible default. Nearest rounds to the closest value, Negative rounds downward, and Positive rounds upward. Try other modes only when a game has known VU1 precision issues such as broken models, bad effects, or scene math problems. Restart the game to apply.

Controls EE/FPU overflow clamping accuracy. None disables the overflow clamp, Normal enables the standard overflow clamp and matches the default, Extra adds stricter overflow handling, and Full enables the strictest EE/FPU clamp behavior. Higher modes can fix specific games with bad CPU floating point edge cases, but may cost performance or change behavior in games that already work correctly. Restart the game to apply.

Controls overflow clamping for Vector Unit 0. None disables VU0 overflow clamping, Normal enables the standard clamp and matches the current VU0 default, Extra adds stricter overflow handling, and Extra+Sign also clamps sign-related overflow behavior. Raise this only for games that specifically need stricter VU0 math; lowering it is mainly useful for testing compatibility or performance regressions. Restart the game to apply.

Controls overflow clamping for Vector Unit 1. None disables VU1 overflow clamping and matches the current VU1 default in this core. Normal enables the standard clamp, Extra adds stricter overflow handling, and Extra+Sign also clamps sign-related overflow behavior. Higher modes can help games with broken geometry, effects, or VU1 vector math, but may reduce speed or affect compatibility in games that do not need them. Restart the game to apply.

Paste one or two direct base URLs. If you use two, put the 2D URL first and the 3D URL second, separated by a space. Leave it empty to use the built-in source again.

EmuCoreR is a PlayStation emulator and game library powered by the PCSX-ReARMed core, with quick setup, clean navigation, and a handheld-friendly interface.
Open the official EmuCoreR website for updates, information, and useful links.
Open the EmuCoreR GitHub repository for the app and project source.
Based on PCSX-ReARMed, an ARM-optimized PlayStation emulator fork by notaz.
Support ongoing development and future updates for EmuCoreR.
Open the author page on Google Play to see other apps from Sashkin Apps.
Enable vibration in supported games and on supported devices.
Runs a short vibration pulse using the current strength slider value.
Vibrate the handheld or phone body when the controller does not expose its own motor.
Play a short haptic tick when pressing on-screen controls.
Play a short vibration tick when pressing physical gamepad buttons.
Use Back button to exit game
Start the exit action instead of opening the game menu when you press Back.
Off by default. When enabled, the Android Back button uses the same exit action as Exit in the game menu, including the current confirmation behavior.
Ask before quick save or quick load.
Hold Triangle + Cross during boot for games with a hidden 480p prompt.
Display the frame rate while playing.
Display the recently played games section on the home screen.
Display the search bar on the home screen.
Show developer profiling tools in the in-game menu.
Log detailed Vulkan/OpenGL GS events to logcat (tag: DebugGS).
Profile EE, IOP, VU0, VU1 execution to logcat (tag: Profiler).
Use English names from the EmuCoreR game database when they are available.
Long-press a setting name to restore that option to its default value.

Choose how a single physical controller should interact with touch controls. Replace touch makes one gamepad take Player 1 immediately, while Touch + Gamepad keeps touch on Player 1 and moves the single gamepad to Player 2. If two physical controllers are connected at the same time, they always become Player 1 and Player 2.

Automatically switches to a connected controller when one is detected. Keep it on if you move between touch controls and a pad often; turn it off only if you want to keep the current input layout fixed.
Prevents Android from dimming or locking the screen during play. Useful for long sessions and games with cutscenes, but it will use a little more battery if you leave the app open.

Lets supported games trigger controller rumble. It adds useful feedback in racing, combat, and impact-heavy games, but it can drain battery faster and some wireless pads may vibrate weakly or with slight delay.
Scales game rumble before it is sent to Android. Lower it for noisy handheld motors, or raise it when a controller feels too weak.
Sends a direct Android vibration request to the connected controller first, then to the phone or handheld fallback when enabled.

Some handheld controls report as a gamepad but expose vibration only through the device vibrator. This fallback keeps rumble working on those devices, but external controllers without rumble will vibrate the phone or handheld instead.
Adds light Android haptic feedback when an on-screen button, D-pad direction, or analog stick is first pressed. This affects control feel only and does not change in-game rumble.
Adds a short low-strength pulse on physical gamepad button presses. This is separate from game rumble, so supported games can still control normal controller vibration.
Shows a confirmation dialog before overwriting a save state or loading one. Turn it off for one-tap quick save and quick load.
Simulates holding Triangle + Cross for a few seconds after launch. Use it for games that reveal a progressive scan or 480p prompt only when this combo is held during boot.
Shows a quick-access row for the games you played last. Good if you bounce between a few titles often; turn it off if you want a cleaner home screen.
Shows the library search bar directly on the home screen. Leave it on for big libraries; turn it off if you prefer a cleaner layout and rarely search by name.
Shows extra diagnostic controls in the in-game menu, including the JIT profiler and hang trace recorder. Keep this off for normal play.

Enables verbose Vulkan/OpenGL graphics synthesizer logging to Android logcat. Filter by tag "DebugGS". Useful only for diagnosing rendering crashes and GPU device lost errors. Keep this off for normal play.
Enables EE, IOP, VU0, VU1 execution profiling to Android logcat. Filter by tag "Profiler". Shows timing for event tests, IOP blocks, DMA interrupts, VU sync. Keep this off for normal play.

Uses English titles from EmuCoreR\'s GameIndex database for games that ship with Japanese or other regional names. This mainly helps imported releases read more clearly in the library, while games without an English database title keep their normal name.
Points EmuCoreR to a clean BIOS dump from your own PlayStation. The image must be exactly 512 KiB and use the .bin or .rom extension.

Adds folders to the game library. EmuCoreR scans every selected folder recursively and merges the results without duplicate file paths. Tap a listed folder to remove it. The current core supports .cue and .bin disc images.

Selects where EmuCoreR stores emulator runtime files such as memory cards, save states, cheats, patches, and logs. Leave it on the default folder unless you want to keep emulator data in a shared or manually managed location.

Chooses the default cover type used when downloading artwork. Flat covers match the classic front-box look, while 3D Box uses angled box renders when the source provides them. 3D covers can look more dramatic, but availability may be slightly worse than flat art.

Overrides the built-in cover source used for automatic downloads. The URL should point directly to a folder that contains JPG covers named by game serial, for example SLUS-20312.jpg. Change this only if you host your own mirror or want to use a different compatible cover library.

Selects the graphics backend used for hardware rendering. Vulkan is usually the fastest on modern devices, OpenGL can be safer for compatibility on some GPUs, and Software is mainly a fallback for testing or games that break badly in hardware mode.

Raises internal render resolution above native PS1 output. 3D scenes look much cleaner, but GPU load climbs fast and some games show extra seams, blur, or broken effects at higher values. If a game looks wrong, switch back to Native first.

Controls how the final image is framed on your display. Auto follows the game, 4:3 keeps the original look for most PS1 titles, 16:9 suits widescreen-patched games, and Stretch should only be used if you do not mind geometric distortion.

Sharpens textures viewed at steep angles, especially roads, floors, fields, and long walls. It usually has a smaller cost than raising resolution, so it is a good quality upgrade if the game already runs well.

Applies a lightweight post-process anti-aliasing pass after rendering. It can smooth jagged edges in games that shimmer, but it also softens UI text and fine detail, so use it only if the cleaner image is worth the blur.

Applies Contrast Adaptive Sharpening after rendering. It is useful if upscaling, FXAA, or bilinear filtering makes the image too soft, but strong sharpening can create halos or noisy edges in some games.

Snapdragon Game Super Resolution reconstructs the image in one mobile-optimized pass without changing the selected internal resolution. Quality processes subtle edges, Balanced uses the official default tuning, and Performance limits reconstruction to stronger edges. While enabled, it replaces CAS and TV presentation shaders.
Sets how aggressive the CAS pass looks. Lower values give a subtle recovery of detail, while higher values make edges pop more but can also introduce ringing and harsh outlines.
Applies a TV-style presentation shader after rendering. Triangular Filter gives a softer CRT-like blend that can look especially good at 2x resolution, but some modes may blur fine UI text.

Loads widescreen patches when the current game has one available. This is usually better than stretching the image because it changes the gameвЂ™s camera and HUD logic instead of just distorting the final picture.
Applies no-interlacing patches where available. This is worth trying in games with combing, shimmer, or flicker from original interlaced output, but availability depends on the title.

Enables internal GS anti-blur handling. This can reduce the blur or flicker caused by alternating PS1 display fields in many games, but it is less exact to original console output and may slightly change some effects.
Changes the size of on-screen buttons and sticks. Increase it if touch accuracy matters more than screen space; lower it if the overlay covers too much of the image.
Controls how solid or transparent the touch controls look. Lower opacity keeps the game view cleaner, while higher opacity makes buttons easier to see in dark or busy scenes.

Makes touch action buttons and shoulder buttons toggle their pressed state with a tap. This is useful for racing games where acceleration needs to stay held, while Start, Select, sticks, and the D-pad keep normal behavior.
Adjusts how quickly the left touch stick reaches stronger movement input. Higher values react faster, while lower values make small movement corrections easier.
Adjusts how quickly the right touch stick reaches stronger input. Higher values make camera or aim changes react faster, while lower values give you finer control.
Inverts the vertical axis for the left analog stick.
Inverts the vertical axis for the right analog stick.
Inverts the horizontal axis for the left analog stick.
Inverts the horizontal axis for the right analog stick.
Ignores small physical stick movements near the center. Raise it if your controller drifts on its own; keep it lower if you want faster response around center.
Adjusts how strongly the physical left stick responds after deadzone processing. Higher values reach full movement faster, while lower values make fine movement easier.
Adjusts how strongly the physical right stick responds after deadzone processing. Higher values make camera or aim movement react faster, while lower values give you finer control.
Maps the R2 analog trigger to upward movement on the right stick for both gamepads and on-screen controls. This can help racing games where throttle is bound to right stick up.
Maps the L2 analog trigger to downward movement on the right stick for both gamepads and on-screen controls. This can help racing games where brake is bound to right stick down.
Hides the touch overlay whenever a physical controller is active. This makes the screen cleaner, but turn it off if you still want touch buttons available while a controller is connected.
Uses a tighter overlay layout that takes less space around the edges of the screen. Good for smaller phones, but some players may prefer the larger spacing of the standard layout.
Changes the size of the analog stick touch areas. Larger values make them easier to grab during action-heavy games, while smaller values leave more room for the picture and nearby buttons.

Applies a tested group of graphics and speed settings in one step. Start here before tuning manually: lower presets favor stability and battery, while faster presets trade image quality or compatibility for speed.

Keeps game speed tied to the selected target frame rate instead of running as fast as possible. Leave it enabled for normal play; disable it only for testing, uncapped behavior, or very specific use cases.

Matches presented frames to the device display refresh. This can reduce tearing, but on some devices or game modes it may cause heavy stalls or slow presentation. Leave it off unless a specific setup benefits from it.

Skips presenting identical frames when the game keeps drawing the same image repeatedly. Leave it enabled for normal play to reduce repeated presents, GPU work, and input latency in many 25/30 FPS titles; turn it off only if a specific game shows worse frame pacing or timing.
Sets the speed target used by the limiter. Most games should stay at their native cap, so change this only if you know the game or patch supports a different target safely.
Sets the base refresh rate used by NTSC-region games when Target FPS is set to Auto. Manual FPS overrides this value while it is enabled.
Sets the base refresh rate used by PAL-region games when Target FPS is set to Auto. Manual FPS overrides this value while it is enabled.

Adjusts how much EE CPU time the emulator gives the game each frame. Lower values can rescue borderline performance on weak devices, but they also make game timing less accurate and can cause slowdown, audio issues, or broken logic.

Lets the emulator skip part of the EE workload to gain speed. It is stronger and riskier than Cycle Rate: useful when a game is close to full speed, but aggressive values can cause stutter, input delay, missing effects, or unstable behavior.
Runs VU1 work on another CPU thread. This often helps on modern multi-core devices, especially in heavier 3D games, but a few titles may show instability or odd timing with it enabled.

Pins the main emulation threads to the fastest CPU cores instead of leaving placement entirely to Android. It can improve stability on powerful chips or cooled handhelds, but may increase heat or reduce performance on some devices if the scheduler would have balanced load better.

Skips the normal BIOS disc boot path and jumps into the game faster. Keep it enabled for most games; turn it off for titles that hang before gameplay, loop on loading screens, or appear to wait forever before the game starts.

Uses looser virtual disc timing to shorten load-related overhead. It can improve performance and reduce long loads in some games, but titles that depend on stricter timing may hang, loop, or fail to load certain scenes correctly.
Fast-forwards tight EE wait loops. Disable this when debugging periodic state jumps, hangs, or games that appear to miss timing-sensitive work.
Optimizes reads from the interrupt status register. Disable this to test games that poll interrupts very closely during startup or cutscenes.
Uses a faster approximation for VU flag timing. Disable this to check for VU state divergence in physics, animation, or camera-heavy scenes.
Runs VU1 work as quickly as possible instead of preserving stricter timing. Disable this to test cutscenes, animation, and games sensitive to VU/GS synchronization.

Controls how the hardware renderer handles GPU readbacks. Faster modes reduce stalls and can help performance in lightweight scenes, but they are more likely to break games that read the framebuffer for shadows, post-processing, or HUD effects. If a game has missing effects, try a safer mode.

Controls how closely hardware rendering matches PS1 alpha blending. Raise it if you see broken fog, halos, light shafts, ghosting, or missing transparency. Lower levels are faster, so leave it low unless the game shows real blending bugs.

Preloads textures before the game asks for them. It can reduce streaming pop-in or stutter in texture-heavy areas, but higher levels use more memory and may do nothing for simpler games. Best left modest unless a game clearly benefits.

Enables mipmaps in the hardware renderer when the game uses them correctly. This can reduce shimmer and improve texture stability in the distance, but a few games have mipmap bugs and may look better with it off.

Drops rendered frames when the device cannot keep up. It can make a slow game feel more playable, but animation becomes rougher and frame pacing gets worse, so it should be a last resort rather than a default tweak.

Loads enabled cheat patches for the current game. Useful for widescreen, fan fixes, translations, or gameplay cheats, but the wrong patch version can break stability or apply to the wrong release of a game.
Shows a live performance overlay while the game is running. Use it when tuning settings or checking whether a slowdown comes from emulation speed, frame pacing, or the game itself.
Chooses between a simple FPS readout and a more detailed stats panel. Use the compact mode if you just want a quick speed check, or the extended mode when you are actively tuning performance.
Places the FPS or stats overlay in one of the four corners. Move it away from touch controls, HUD elements, subtitles, or minimaps so it stays readable without covering important game info.

Allows you to select a custom GPU driver package (like Turnip) to replace the default system driver. Custom drivers can significantly improve performance or fix visual glitches in certain games on Snapdragon/Adreno devices. If you experience crashes, revert to the System driver.
Selects the mobile GPU branch used by hardware rendering. Snapdragon keeps the current Adreno path; MediaTek exposes Mali and PowerVR fixes for devices that need those GPU paths.

Routes the MediaTek OpenGL renderer through bundled ANGLE libraries. Because of translation overhead, this might increase or decrease performance depending on the game. Available for Mali and PowerVR profiles and stays off by default.

Controls the main texture filtering mode used by the renderer. Nearest keeps the sharpest raw look, PS1 stays closest to original console behavior, and Forced modes smooth more aggressively. If a game looks too blocky or too blurry, this is the first filtering option to adjust.

Controls how textures are filtered before they reach the screen. PS1/Automatic modes stay closer to original behavior, Forced modes smooth everything, and Nearest keeps the sharpest but roughest image. If a game looks too blurry or too noisy, this is one of the first options to try.

Smooths transitions between mip levels on textures that use them. It can reduce shimmer on roads, walls, and distant surfaces, but stronger modes may blur the image more than the original game intended.

Sets the sprite size threshold where draws start moving to the CPU path. This is mainly useful for games with broken 2D effects, shadows, or post-processing at higher resolutions. Raising it can fix more issues, but it costs CPU performance quickly.
Controls how aggressively sprite rendering is offloaded to the CPU. Higher levels can repair more sprite-based effects, but they are heavier and should usually be used only as a per-game fix.

Processes CLUT and palette work through a software path instead of the usual GPU route. Useful for wrong colors, broken gradients, subtitles, or palette-heavy 2D games, but slower than normal hardware rendering.

Controls whether the renderer builds CLUT textures directly from GPU targets. Safer modes help games that render their palettes into textures first; faster modes reduce overhead but can miss those effects.

Flushes hardware draws more often so later passes can read a finished result. It often helps missing bloom, shadows, framebuffer effects, or bad layering, but it can hurt performance a lot if left on globally.

Skips draw calls from the start of a chosen range. Use it only for specific games with black boxes, ghost layers, broken blur, or bad post-processing. Start low and increase carefully, because it can also remove effects you actually want.
Sets the end of the skipped draw-call range. It works together with Skip Draw Start and is meant for surgical, game-specific fixes rather than general tuning.

Changes how the hardware renderer detects textures stored inside render targets. This can fix missing HUDs, videos, or framebuffer-based effects in some games, but stronger modes are heavier and should only be used when needed.

Adjusts sampling to compensate for half-pixel rounding differences between the PS1 and modern graphics APIs. It is often the first fix to try for shifted bloom, double images, outlines, or post-processing that looks offset when upscaling.

Keeps certain sprite and 2D draws closer to native PS1 scaling even when the game is rendered above native resolution. This can help HUD alignment, text, and post-process layers that only break when the image is upscaled.
Rounds sprite coordinates to reduce thin seams, gaps, or flickering lines on 2D elements and HUDs. It is especially useful in games that show grid lines only when rendered above native resolution.
Applies bilinear filtering to upscale passes used by some effects. It can smooth harsh scaling artifacts in post-process layers, but it may also soften the image more than you want.
Offsets texture sampling horizontally. This is a precision fix for games where text, HUDs, or post-process layers appear shifted left or right after upscaling.
Offsets texture sampling vertically. Use it only when a game shows layers, HUD elements, or effects shifted up or down after changing resolution.

Moves 4-bit and 8-bit framebuffer conversion from the GPU to the CPU. This can fix some HUDs, shadows, FMV overlays, and other framebuffer tricks, but it is expensive and is best used only for games that clearly need it.

Stops depth data from being converted in the texture cache. It can fix a few games with incorrect lighting, dark scenes, or performance drops, but it may also break effects that rely on correct depth information.

Turns off conservative safety checks in the hardware renderer. It can help with oversized effects, thick outlines, or upscaling glitches in a few games, but it also increases the chance of new rendering bugs. Leave it off unless you are fixing a specific issue.

Disables automatic per-game render fixes from the core. Usually you should leave this off, because those fixes exist for a reason. Turn it on only if an automatic fix is clearly causing a new problem and you want to test without it.

Uploads GS memory at the start of the frame instead of waiting for the effect to request it later. This can fix difficult framebuffer effects such as missing lava, heat haze, or special blending, but it increases bandwidth and may reduce performance.

Invalidates the whole overlapping texture region instead of only the intersected part. This can help games with stale textures, broken post-processing, or framebuffer feedback issues, but it is heavier on bandwidth and cache use.

Forces render targets back to local memory when they are closed. Useful for games that lose effects after scene changes, menus, or transitions, but it is slower and usually only worth enabling per game.
Guesses the real size of textures when the game does not define the region properly. It can fix stretched, oversized, or garbage textures, but if the guess is wrong it can create new artifacts.

Moves palette conversion work from the CPU to the GPU. It is usually faster, especially in palette-heavy 2D games, but if a title shows wrong colors or broken CLUT effects, try the safer path instead.

Adjusts sprite placement to hide thin vertical seams that appear when 2D elements are upscaled. This is one of the classic fixes for UI lines, menu borders, and sprite edges in games that are otherwise fine at native resolution.

Combines neighboring post-process sprites into a larger draw so bloom, blur, and similar fullscreen effects line up better when upscaled. It can fix split or duplicated effects, but sometimes it over-corrects and changes the look.
Snaps sprite positions to even coordinates to reduce tiny gaps or shimmering between pixels at higher resolutions. Helpful for 2D-heavy games, but it can slightly shift some elements.

Draws palette-based effects closer to native precision. This can repair color-indexed effects, palette shadows, or other CLUT-heavy tricks that break when upscaled, but it may also make high-resolution output look less clean.
Use a tighter layout for on-screen controls.
Prevent the screen from dimming while playing.
Changes the text size of both the simple FPS counter and detailed statistics. Larger values also widen the detailed overlay to reduce wrapping.
Choose the individual values included in the detailed statistics overlay. App, build, and core versions are always shown first. GPU timing is collected only while the GPU metric is selected.
Use PNG and DDS files from each game serial folder.
Load replacement textures on a worker thread while the game runs.
Load the full pack up front. Faster in-game lookups, but heavier on startup and memory.
Save detected game textures into the dumps folder for pack creation.
Import a ZIP with a PS1 serial folder or a replacements folder. The storage path above follows your selected emulator folder.
Delete all replacements and dumps for %s?
Delete dumped textures for %s and keep replacements?
Tap action and shoulder buttons to hold them, then tap again to release.
Invert vertical movement on the left analog stick.
Invert horizontal movement on the left analog stick.
Invert vertical movement on the right analog stick.
Invert horizontal movement on the right analog stick.
Connect a gamepad to adjust physical stick settings.
Use R2 as right stick up.
Use L2 as right stick down.
Choose whether one connected gamepad replaces touch controls or works alongside them.
Keeps your manual tuning. The preset switches back to Custom when you change a tuned option.
Lower heat and power draw. Best for long sessions on weaker MediaTek devices.
Recommended starting point for most MediaTek devices. Good image quality without heavy speed hacks.
Adds moderate speed hacks and keeps image quality solid. Good when Balanced is close but not stable enough.
Pushes speed hacks harder for difficult games. Faster, but more likely to cause glitches or unstable timing.
Allows the core to load active cheats from pnach files.
Add a .pnach file and manage it directly in the app.
Tip: use .pnach files named by CRC, serial + CRC, serial, or game title. Imported cheats are enabled automatically and can be toggled in the in-game menu.
This adjusts renderer and safe speedhacks for the current device family without hardcoding per-game hacks.
Recommended for MediaTek: switches to OpenGL, keeps native resolution, lowers filtering load, and uses safer speedhacks to reduce crashes and improve frame pacing.
Recommended for Snapdragon: keeps the fast default path and reapplies the balanced preset for stable performance.
Applies a balanced compatibility preset for devices that do not have a chipset-specific profile yet.
Uses a second thread for VU1 - speeds up most games
Keeps EE, VU1, and GS work on the fastest CPU cores when supported.
Skips the BIOS disc boot - disable for games that hang before starting
Faster disc access - may cause issues in some games
Runs VU1 work with looser timing
Changes synchronization behavior for hardware GS downloads. No Readbacks is the balanced Android default; Asynchronous is experimental and returns the latest completed GPU data.
Keeps the game closer to the selected target speed instead of running fully uncapped.
Synchronizes frame presentation with the display refresh rate.
Sets the speed used while holding Start for fast-forward.
Avoids presenting identical frames multiple times in a row.
Enables emulation of the GS texture mipmapping path.
Convert 4-bit and 8-bit framebuffers on the CPU instead of the GPU.
Turns off depth buffer support in the texture cache.
Turns off several conservative safety checks for speed.
Disables automatic per-game render fixes from the core.

Aim converts phone rotation speed into the right analog stick for camera control in shooters and automatically returns to center when the phone stops moving. Steering converts the phoneвЂ™s held tilt into the left analog stick for racing games and calibrates the current angle as center when gameplay starts. The selected mode is used only while a game is running and requires the corresponding motion sensor.
Controls how strongly phone movement deflects the emulated analog stick. Per-game overrides are recommended because games use different camera and steering response curves.
Filters sensor noise and hand shake. Lower values react faster; higher values feel steadier but add a small amount of latency.

Linear interpolation, no Time Stretch, and simplified effects

Off by default. Reduces audio CPU usage by using Linear interpolation, disabling Time Stretch, and bypassing SPU2 reverb. Audio may sound flatter or crackle if the game cannot maintain full speed. Your manual processing settings are restored when this mode is turned off.

AAudio provides low latency but may stutter on slower or heavily loaded devices. OpenSL ES uses a simpler buffer queue and is more stable on weaker hardware, at the cost of slightly higher latency. Changing this setting requires restarting the game.
Use the lowest latency supported by the audio device
Controls audio volume during normal emulation.
Controls audio volume while fast-forward is active.
Mutes emulator audio without changing the saved volume levels.
Selects how SPU2 voice samples are reconstructed. Gaussian matches PlayStation hardware and is the recommended default; other methods can change sound character or reduce processing cost.
TimeStretch keeps audio synchronized when emulation speed fluctuates. Disabling synchronization can reduce processing but may cause crackling, pitch changes, or gaps.
Controls how much generated audio is buffered. Larger values reduce crackling but increase latency. The default is 100 ms.
Lets Android select a small burst-aligned output buffer. Disable this option to set output latency manually.
Controls the audio device buffer separately from the emulator buffer. Lower values reduce delay but may crackle on slower devices.

Disable CPU/GTE pipeline stalls. Speed hack that may break timing-sensitive games.
Emulate exceptions precisely in interpreter mode. Improves accuracy at the cost of speed.

Soft is gentle, Balanced is the natural default, Crisp is short and precise, and Strong is deeper for weaker vibration motors.
